entry.title: ‘Wildwood’ Director Travis Knight on How Live-Action Filmmaking Shaped His Stop-Motion Animated Adventure
entry.summary: Director Travis Knight tells IndieWire about bringing techniques he learned from live action to Laika's stop-motion epic adventure story.
entry.content:
Many scenes in “Wildwood” are designed to look spectacular. Even if each frame weren’t already rendered with the meticulous detail and artistry of stop-motion animation, the Laika Studios film is full of complex, chaotic battle sequences, a forest writhing with eldritch magic, and giant eagles soaring through the sky.

But some of the most technically challenging scenes, according to director Travis Knight, aren’t the ones that look the most majestic. They are — true to the spirit of the film and the lesson learned by its stubborn, caring protagonist Prue (Peyton Elizabeth Lee) — the simple magic of everyday life.

Related Stories
‘Club Kid’ Review: Jordan Firstman’s Brazen, Funny, and Surprisingly Earnest Directing Debut Is a Wild Party Movie with Heart
‘Being Heumann’ Review: Siân Heder’s ‘CODA’ Follow-Up Is an Essential Biopic That’s Not Afraid to Have Some Fun

In fact, Knight told IndieWire on an episode of the Filmmaker Toolkit podcast that one of the most challenging sequences in “Wildwood” was simply getting its hero from one end of her bedroom to the other. Laika prefers Canon cameras mounted on large motion-control rigs, which offer the flexibility needed to capture puppet movements adjusted one frame at a time. But when the camera moves, it also has to do so one painstaking frame at a time.

Knight, who’s now directed live-action features “Bumblebee” and “Masters of the Universe” in addition to his Laika work on “Kubo and the Two Strings,” wanted “Wildwood” to have the same camera language as a live-action film. He wanted the intimacy and wordless visual storytelling of a camera tracking Prue as she huffs across her bedroom, where the camera movement helps us see the decor shift from the artifacts of a carefree kid to those of a more disaffected teen.

“I still wanted it to feel like it was shot like a live-action film, with that kind of intimacy with the camera. But a camera on a motion-control rig is the size of a Ford F-150 in our [puppet-scale] world. It’s huge. And so if a camera is moving, you have to create space for the camera on set,” Knight said.

This is on top of creating space for the animator, who is roughly the size of a Kaiju in comparison to the fifth-scale the humans on either side of the Impassable Wood live at. The Prue puppet is roughly 10 inches tall. Being able to move that puppet and a camera at least as large as her bedroom that the puppet is moving through? That is a particularly gnarly feat of physics.

“We essentially had to deconstruct the set,” Knight said. “It was almost like it was a clamshell. It would open to make room for the camera, and then it would close up again. It was such a complicated engineering feat, when all it is [for] is a camera panning across a room. Those are the kinds of challenges that the team has to figure out, which is stupid, but it’s what it requires if you’re trying to tell a story like this.”

There is much to be said, and rightly, about the awe-inducing moments of spectacle in “Wildwood.” The Laika team had to figure out how to make giant puppets out of fabric and feathers instead of standard-issue silicone to simulate flight compellingly, accurately, and tactilely. Combat sequences required enormous attention to detail. But when Knight watches the film, he’s just as struck by the invisible work that makes “Wildwood” feel like a live-action epic — the thankless but involving work that viewers aren’t ever meant to see.

“I learned a great many things about what to do, what not to do [working in live-action]. It fundamentally changed my relationship with the camera, which is one of the reasons why ‘Wildwood’ looks so different. It’s because I wanted it to feel as if it were without the inherent limitations you would typically find in stop-motion cinematography,” Knight said. “When I see this movie, I am seeing all these little miraculous moments of engineering and artistry and human creativity at play on the big screen, and that’s one of the reasons it moves me so much.”

“Wildwood” is now playing in theaters.

entry.title: ‘Club Kid’ Review: Jordan Firstman’s Brazen, Funny, and Surprisingly Earnest Directing Debut Is a Wild Party Movie with Heart
entry.summary: Comedian/actor Jordan Firstman makes his auspicious directing debut with the brazen, only-in-New-York comedy 'Club Kid.' Review.
entry.content:
[Editor’s note: This review was originally published on May 15, 2026 during the 2026 Cannes Film Festival. A24 will release “Club Kid” in theaters on Friday, November 6.]

Ask any gay man with a social media account, and they likely have an opinion about Jordan Firstman. The backlash-courting queer actor/comedian, controversial most recently because of an online flare-up over querying the sexual realism of “Heated Rivalry,” is labeled either candid or confrontational. He also has a record of taking on sexually explicit projects like Sebastian Silva’s suicide-ideating, ketamine-fueled dark comedy “Rotting in the Sun.” His status as a self-aware, hyper-online provocateur may not seem to suggest the makings of a bona fide filmmaker, but just wait.

Related Stories
‘Being Heumann’ Review: Siân Heder’s ‘CODA’ Follow-Up Is an Essential Biopic That’s Not Afraid to Have Some Fun
Will Brill Won a Tony and Got His First Leading Film Role, but That’s Not How He Measures Success

While that reputation might have Firstman on guard as he debuts his feature writing/directing debut “Club Kid,” as it will certain circumspect corners of the audience, this terrific movie should put any of those nervous feelings to rest. Even his haters won’t be able to resist what’s announced here as a major filmmaking talent with a sensitive side that belies his brash, internet-based persona.

He also stars as the protagonist of his hugely crowd-pleasing, excruciatingly funny, and poignant first film — one that plays to all sides of the room despite being brazenly, unapologetically queer — which will prime Firstman-savvy viewers to immediately interpret “Club Kid” as autobiographical. That’s because it is.

He plays party promoter Peter, now in his thirties after a decade-plus of MDMA-addled revelry, the kind where all the days blur and blot into one long and sweaty night with a coming horizon in the shape of regret. Firstman may not be playing himself this time, but he is playing a version of that self, having, as he says, spent enough years in Berlin to be labeled “the angel of Berghain” by his new friends, but now ready to put the days-that-became-years of GHB, MDMA, and other letters of the alphabet behind him.

“Club Kid” is exactly about what happens when the lights go up on the party, the shameover of the morning after that becomes a way of being, and the need to do it all over again to stave off last night’s aching after effects. But it’s also about — earnesty alert! — family lost and found, not only because of the queer community formed around the now-orphaned Peter, who lives in the rent-controlled Manhattan his mother left him after she died, but because he wakes up one day to find a child he fathered and never knew about, literally on his doorstep.

“Club Kid” was shot on 35mm on location in New York City with a team of backers including “Anora” Oscar-winning producer Alex Coco and nepo filmmaker Olmo Schnabel, and a millennial cast of queer comedians. So it’s hard not to leave the movie thinking all that’s needed here is an A24 logo slapped onto the opening credits, and it’s ready for the world. But no matter; while Firstman’s aesthetic is loudly in A24’s register, it turns out to be an asset rather than a limitation.

Beginning inside a sensually lit, drug-soaked party and ending as one rages on without you from afar, “Club Kid” drops us into Brooklyn 2016. Peter, sing-screaming Rihanna’s “Sex with Me” in a clown car of an Uber ride with his friends, is headed into yet another bender to remember (but also eventually forget). At a club of the sort that now dominates night culture in Bushwick, rising party promoter Peter ends up hooking up — and then really hooking up — with a couple of hyperactive “innit, babes?” British women in the back room. It’s all inconspicuously taking a turn for the sexual when the movie smash cuts to “a decade or so later,” when the proverbial party is still dying down, but Peter is still living in it — albeit more sweaty and tragic 10 years on.

He’s now made a career out of his drug use with his best friend and business partner Sophie (a marvelous, perpetually coked-out Cara Delevingne, who’s two inches from a breakdown at all times). A few days before the one that’s about to change his life, they have an important sit-down coming up with FiDi investors to help expand their New York party empire. But alas, as he couldn’t help himself once again the night before, Peter wakes up drugged to the gills, rushing to the meeting only to nod off at the table, still in a GHB-spiked stupor. (His reaction to a dropper of hot sauce that looks curiously similar to the one he used last night to get high is one of the film’s many brilliantly funny little pratfalls.)  

All of that’s to say Peter’s life is still totally a mess, and his arrested development from a decade of partying has now washed him out to the point where sobriety is maybe never part of his day. (A weekend spent dissipated, hungover, jerking off to internet porn and eating Popeye’s in bed rings painfully true.)

Party’s certainly over, though, when one of those British “innit babes” from 10 years ago, Edison (Kirby Howell-Baptiste), shows up from London at his apartment (where Peter lives with an “Azerbaijanian aspiring queer philosopher” who doesn’t pay rent) with an eight-year-old boy. “You’ve got a kid! ‘Yay!,’” she tells him while delivering the news that Arlo (preternaturally gifted young breakout actor Reggie Absalom) is in fact Peter’s child with one of the other women from that opening-scene heterosexual encounter, who’s just died. The first and only time Peter fucked a woman, and now he’s fucked himself into having to finish raising a small boy.

Cue the manic panic, more drug use, and resignation to the idea that there’s no sending this kid back to the U.K.

While it’s a bit sudden how fast the switch flips from Peter feeling wildly ill-equipped for parenting to becoming a nurturing caretaker, he and Arlo turn out to have more in common than not. Arlo, for one, has the music taste of someone who grew up on Pitchfork, eagerly taking to the $300 Elliott Smith record Peter buys for him in a later scene. (The soundtrack on this thing, by the way, rules, from Arthur Russell during the film’s melancholy final act to “The White Lotus” composer Cristobal Tapia de Veer’s deeply felt original score.) Their relationship, however quickly, becomes the film’s so-far unexpected sweet center, as Peter starts to really appreciate and eventually love Arlo, who has traumas of his own.

A lot of the success of “Club Kid” rides not only on Firstman’s shoulders, but also on the collaborators he’s working with, including cinematographer Adam Newport-Berra who captures a certain lost-era grit in New York as well as in the chaos-packed nightclub sequences. “Club Kid” also takes advantage of New York City as not just a backdrop but a central character in the storytelling, using the city in a way that feels rare onscreen these days.

“Club Kid” freewheels and unwinds like a head rush of a zippy party movie until Arlo’s introduction brings the comedown. It turns out he feels more at home among Peter’s “found family” of queer revelers, discovering his own DJ skills in the process, than he ever did in London. Could Peter really warm to fatherhood? Real emotional stakes start to heighten as he begins recognizing the unexpected realities of his new arrangement, like getting Arlo into school, or keeping the boy shielded from the drug use of his friends while Peter’s own finally starts to diminish. A nervous, tentative romance comes into view with child psychologist Oscar (Diego Calva), and on a date where a namecheck of Gregg Araki’s “Mysterious Skin” becomes not just a tender confession, but a turn-on.  

“Club Kid” takes a sharp dramatic turn, in which the nature of Arlo’s living situation becomes even more dire and probably illegal, that almost shouldn’t work in a comedy like this — but it’s a turn that feels inevitable given how “Club Kid” is structured like the rise and fall of a drug experience, a high that crashes down into despair. The emotional arc bends toward “Kramer vs. Kramer” territory with a cathartic (and well-played by Firstman) courtroom oner. Peter may be insecure about his own place in a world where only parts of it have room for him, but as a storyteller with an eye, Firstman is anything but.

Firstman is by now an established comedic voice, but his work on all sides of the camera here leaves pretty of room for revelation, for him to become a genuine discovery beyond an audience of gay, internet-addled millennials. “Club Kid” has real potential to break out bigger than its seemingly niche scope would suggest, with Firstman finally shirking the ironic pose he’s taken online for years to emerge as a sincere storyteller with heart as much as humor.

Grade: A-

“Club Kid” premiered at the 2026 Cannes Film Festival. It is currently seeking U.S. distribution.

entry.title: ‘Being Heumann’ Review: Siân Heder’s ‘CODA’ Follow-Up Is an Essential Biopic That’s Not Afraid to Have Some Fun
entry.summary: TIFF: Heder's look at a remarkable period in activist Judy Heumann's work is life-affirming in myriad ways, and boasts a star turn from Ruth Madeley.
entry.content:
[Editor’s note: This review was originally published on September 10, 2026 during the 2026 Toronto International Film Festival. Apple will release the film in select theaters on Friday, November 6 and on Apple TV on Friday, November 13.]

When Siân Heder’s “CODA” premiered at Sundance in 2021 (during the festival’s online-only “pandemic year” and months and months before the film would go on to win Best Picture), it became an early favorite of mine. Mostly, I wrote in my review, though the “drama is marked by familiar beats, its characters bring new dimension to a staid genre.” The same can be said about Heder’s follow-up feature, “Being Heumann,” which brings real life back to the biopic, not only through innumerable compelling characters, but the smart choice to tightly focus this story on one essential moment in the life of the activist Judy Heumann.

Related Stories
Will Brill Won a Tony and Got His First Leading Film Role, but That’s Not How He Measures Success
‘Cherry & Virgin’ Review: A Fantastic Indie Anime Blends Different Art Styles and a Slew of Pop Culture References into an Innovative Modern Rom-Com

When we first meet Judy (Ruth Madeley in a true star turn), she’s zipping along a busy New York City street in 1972. That might sound fun, but for Judy, it’s just the way things are; a wheelchair user since she was just a toddler (thanks to an early bout with polio), the world is not made for people like Judy, and she makes her way through it however she can. Often, that means doing things like, oh, zipping down city streets, because there are no curb cuts to assist her in smoothly moving from sidewalk to sidewalk. As Judy goes barreling down the street, people stare, drivers yell, and the brassy Brooklynite throws up a finger.

That Judy has natural presence is a given, but the central question of Heder’s film — which she adapted from Heumann’s autobiography alongside co-writer Rebekah Taussig — is how she will use all that verve to truly enact change. It’s the sort of concern that has always impacted great leaders, and suffice it to say, Heumann was indeed a great leader. But while Heumann’s long, storied life had many incredible chapters (she passed away in 2023, two years after she started working with Heder on the film), the filmmakers smartly zero in one on seminal slice of life to craft “Being Heumann.” Cradle to the grave this is not, but the film still succeeds mightily when contextualizing Heumann’s role in the disability rights movement and her singularity as a true American original.

That’s not to say that the period of time covered by the film — which soon jumps ahead five years — isn’t complicated and dense. The film opens in 1972, because that’s when Judy and eighty other activists staged a sit-in on Madison Avenue to protest the vetoing of Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act, which we’re told was one of the very first pieces of federal legislation meant to guarantee certain rights to people with disabilities (from accessibility to education). The act was eventually signed in 1973, but when the film picks back up in 1978, it has not been implemented. It needed one last step: a signature from newly-installed Secretary of Health, Education, and Welfare Joseph Califano (Mark Ruffalo). And he wasn’t signing.

Heder and Taussig’s script distills the legal wrangling down well: this piece of legislation will help bring about massive positive change for the disabled community, but it will cost a lot of money, and Califano has already been asked to slash the budget. These are excellent stakes.

Judy doesn’t care about the cost to the government — why should she? — but she does care about the cost to her community. A seasoned and dogged activist, most of the people in Judy’s life are disabled in some way, and it’s her mission to a) wrangle them into action and b) be pretty pushy about it. Heder and her casting directors Bernard Telsey and Adam Caldwell have assembled a wonderful, winning cast around Madeley (herself a wheelchair user), including a number of disabled performers, cast here as icons in their own right. Standouts include Madeline Delp as Kitty Cone (the honey to Judy’s vinegar), Andrew Pilkington as Hale Zukas, Antwan Tolliver as Brad Lomax, “CODA” star Daniel Durant as Steve McCleeland, Roberta Colindrez as Joni Breves, and instant star Charlie Rush-Reese as Dennis Billups.

That Heder would cast actually disabled people in these roles should seem obvious (this is the filmmaker behind “CODA,” after all), but there’s no question that it totally pays off all the same. The wide array of performers on offer here is thrilling, and it’s a treat to see them all settling in so well to this period world, rendered tactile and realistic by smart costuming choices by Danny Glicker and unfussy production design by John P. Goldsmith.

Enraged over the lack of movement on the signing of 504, Judy and her compatriots launch a series of protests around the country, focused on federal buildings that house HEW offices. Califano, stuck back in DC, can only hear about these events as they unfold, utterly stymied but what to do, paralyzed by fear for his job, and intent on reminding people he’s one of the good guys (he supported the Selma marches!). But the world has changed. When Judy somewhat impulsively leads a pack of protesters inside the SF federal building, what follows will only spark further change.

Despite the historical implications that follow — the SF sit-in became one of the country’s largest — Heder doesn’t noodle on the cultural vegetable aspect of this story. Instead, “Being Heumann” becomes something unexpectedly frisky and fun. The sit-in comes with plenty of challenges (beyond the myriad needs of the disabled community, there’s in-fighting to spare, government pressures galore, and deep worries about how it might actually pan out), but there’s also a streak of joy that runs through it. It’s thrilling to see people doing literally whatever they can for their well-being, and having a good time in the process (yes, you’ll get acquainted with their “sex tents” soon enough). There are almost too many colorful characters here, a sprawling ensemble in which everyone deserves their own film, though we occasionally lose some threads along the way.

That isn’t always easy for Judy, though, who remains set in her ways even as she sees real change happening around her. Madeley captures the real Judy Heumann’s energy beautifully; she’s funny and flinty and spiky and smarter than anyone else around her and totally driven by her sense of justice and equality. But that’s not always enough, a lesson that “Being Heumann” is not shy about. Fighting for what’s right involves just that, fighting. Sometimes, that even means fighting your own instincts.

A film like ”Being Heumann” is destined to be called rousing — a call to action that’s every bit as entertaining as it is inspiring. It’s a film about tough choices and even tougher circumstances, but it’s also about the tangible good that can come from people working together. What could be more joyous than that? More biopics could learn from this formula, and from this feeling. Be more like Judy: be tough, but never be afraid of joy.

Grade: B+

“Being Heumann” premiered at the 2026 Toronto International Film Festival. Apple will release it in select theaters on Friday, November 6 and on Apple TV on Friday, November 13.

entry.title: Will Brill Won a Tony and Got His First Leading Film Role, but That’s Not How He Measures Success
entry.summary: INTERVIEW: The "Stereophonic" winner, "The Musical" lead, and supporting star on "Being Heumann" tells IndieWire what real creative joy looks like.
entry.content:
It’s all glamorous — chatting Tony wins and snagging leading roles in movies and sterling New York Times reviews — until your cat needs something. Fortunately, actor Will Brill knows a thing or two about balance, and managed to both a) charmingly answer our many varied queries about his wide-ranging career and b) attend to his yowling tabby’s needs while doing so.

Brill is one of those actors you know, even if you don’t know him by name. One of the “oh, I love that guy!” kind of performers. The kind of performer who shows up and instantly makes things better, or brighter, or somehow richer. His credits are wide and deep — movies like “Caught Stealing” and “Test Pattern,” shows like “The OA” and “The Marvelous Mrs. Maisel,” theater like “Oklahoma” and “Stereophonic” — and things are only picking up for him.

Related Stories
‘Cherry & Virgin’ Review: A Fantastic Indie Anime Blends Different Art Styles and a Slew of Pop Culture References into an Innovative Modern Rom-Com
Alan Cumming Says ‘Tip Toe’ Was His Greatest Role Ever — but He Never Wants to Think About It Again

In 2024, Brill won his first Tony for the beloved rock musical “Stereophonic,” snagging Best Featured Actor in a Play in a field that included two of his own co-stars. In 2025, he got his first leading role in the film, care of Giselle Bonilla’s darkly hilarious “The Musical.” Not too shabby, right? It gets better.

When Brill spoke with IndieWire, reviews were just hitting for the limited run of “Kramer/Fauci” at St. Ann’s Warehouse. Daniel Fish’s lauded play previously ran at the Skirball earlier this year and, this fall, Brill reprised his role as, yes, that Dr. Anthony Fauci. The creative, thrilling play dramatizes a 1993 C-SPAN call-in show, during which Fauci (then the director of the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases) and Larry Kramer (the famously outspoken playwright and activist) went at each other over the plans for a new government task force on H.I.V. and AIDS.

“I’m one of those weirdos who will read [reviews],” Brill said with a laugh when asked if he’d been keeping up with the glowing criticism for the show. “I read every single review. I’ve read every review of ‘The Musical’ on Letterboxd. Some would say I’m a glutton for punishment.”

Helen Shaw’s review in the New York Times, he agreed, was not punishment. “I felt auspicious because I knew that Helen Shaw had seen it at Skirball and really enjoyed it,” he said. “But, even so, to say, ‘The most beautiful play I’ve seen all year and I would happily see it 10 more times’ is crazy. I mean, it’s so cool.”

Brill has been doing live theater as long as he’s been acting, getting his start in children’s theater when he was still just a kid in the Bay Area. Process is compelling to him, and he lights up when asked about something as workaday as what he does during the hours between demanding shows.

“It depends on the show a lot, the difference between this show and ‘Stereophonic,’ for instance, is that Stereophonic was a three-hour, 15-minute show where I was screaming and crying most of the times that I was on stage, and this show is an hour long and I never have to raise my voice,” Brill said. “I get to lie down for part of it! Also, for ‘Stereophonic,’ we were in Midtown Manhattan, and for this, I’m in Dumbo, so I get to go outside and sit by the river and read my book, which is dreamy. And then during ‘Stereophonic,’—”

That’s when Curtis the tabby really gets going. “Sorry, my cat is really going through it. Can you hear him?,” Brill said, before darting off-screen to retrieve and present a gorgeous and giant striped feline. “This is Curtis. What is it, baby? He’s screaming. He’s been walking around screaming his head off. Oh, I wonder … I have a robot litter box now and it looks like it is… Sorry, this is such a chaotic morning for me. I think it just needs a reset. Maybe that’s what’s going on with him.”

Yowling cats will keep anyone grounded. In a weird way, so will Tony wins. I asked Brill what changed — or didn’t — after he won his first.

“I think less changed than I sort of expected it would,” he said. “There’s all kinds of legends about what people go through, what changes for people. Oh, my gosh, people love to say, ‘Oh, I thought my entire career was going to change and then I didn’t work for three years.’ And that was certainly not the case for me, but I did have to make a pretty difficult choice about whether or not I was going to go do the show again in London, which I ultimately decided not to do. I had a year where I made less money than I would have, but I did some really rewarding and very challenging things. I starred in a movie for the first time. I had never done that before, so that was really exciting and new and different.”

Bonilla’s feature debut “The Musical” debuted at this year’s Sundance Film Festival and was recently released in theaters and on VOD. It’s a tricky film to explain — it has a twist, sort of, but really just a devilish sense of humor — and Brill loved that. He stars as middle school drama teacher Doug Leibowitz, recently dumped his girlfriend, consumed by his failures as a playwright, and perhaps in the exact right mental headspace to put on an, ahem, shocking new musical.

“I wish I could remember when exactly it dawned on me in the script, because definitely it took me by surprise and it was at that moment where I thought, ‘Oh, I have to do this. There’s no question about this. This is my role,’” he said when asked about the moment he realized what the film was doing with its central musical conceit. “Because it was so exciting and so unlike anything else that I had read. Giselle and I would sneak in to screenings to hear the audience realize what’s happening and listen to them respond to it, and it’s always terribly gratifying.”

We won’t spoil the film here, but suffice to say, Doug and his merry band of middle schoolers put on a show that is based on perhaps the last event you’d ever expect to inspire a musical. The first time Brill saw the film with an audience who had no idea what they were in for, he realized going in cold might be the move.

“I realized that really the best way to experience the movie is with other people not knowing what is coming, because the shock is so crazy,” he said. “And something about the way that it has been finagled is that you are pulled in so many directions, between wanting Doug to fail, but also wanting the children to succeed. It’s such a torrent of things happening that it’s really sort of best to experience with a bunch of other people at the same time.”

The role might have been Brill’s first leading one on the big screen, but he’s no stranger to tough material — or the weight of it. In 2019, he starred alongside Brittany S. Hall in Shatara Michelle Ford’s staggering debut feature, “Test Pattern.” The film follows couple Renesha (Hall) and Evan (Brill) as they navigate a horrific sexual assault and a system not at all equipped to handling survivors with grace.

“They share more DNA than you would think,” he said of Bonilla’s film and Ford’s. “‘Test Pattern’ was the biggest emotional undertaking that I’d ever taken on film before. I was being trusted with a lot by Shatara. They were also a first-time filmmaker, so there was a lot of trust that we were giving to each other, and that was very palpable from the first time we met each other, that we were embarking on something that was pretty untrod territory for both of us and maybe in the landscape of cinema. We both felt tremendous responsibility. We both took it very, very seriously and were asking a lot of ourselves and each other.”

Ford’s film was made “on a shoestring budget” with “absolutely no amenities of any kind,” the actor added. “But that said, it was really rewarding, and everybody showed up really desperate to do well every day,” he said. “Similarly, on ‘The Musical,’ I’m on camera in almost every scene of the movie, so I felt a lot of pressure at the time. I knew that a lot of the success of the thing relied on me, and usually, at least in my career, that’s not been the case. I’ve played a lot of supporting roles, and I know that I can show up for a scene and deliver something special and ultimately get to walk away and say, ‘This thing does not live or die on my performance alone.’ I couldn’t write that off with either of the two movies.”

Brill has also dipped into studio features, including a small but memorable role in Darren Aronofsky’s 2025 crime dramedy “Caught Stealing,” in which he plays a homeless man who offers a surprising key to a complicated story.

“Those experiences are wild, because you walk onyo the set and it’s you and Austin Butler and Zoe Kravitz and Darren Aronofsky,” he said. “And you’re just sort of like, ‘OK…’ It’s a lot of pressure, and it’s a lot of excitement. ‘Test Pattern’ had a crew of 20 people on any given day, and then there were 100 or more people on the set of ‘Caught Stealing’ every time I was there. We were shutting down blocks of New York City traffic for hours in the middle of the night. It was really wild.”

The role might have been firmly supporting, but the experience really stuck with him. “I had two very big votes of confidence while I was working on that movie that I felt really cool about,” the actor said. “One was that when pedestrians got hustled by. on more than one occasion, people were like, ‘Why aren’t they moving this homeless man who’s on the street?’ People had to be like ‘He’s an actor.’ So that felt really good. I got sort of nervous that I was going to be there in the presence of this auteur who was going to be self-serious and formidable and difficult, and Darren was everything you want a director to be. He was so game, he was so fun. He was appreciating the magic of every moment, and he was so supportive of his actors. Every time I did a take, he was like, ‘Oh my God, this is so much fun. I wish we had you for longer.’ It’s very cool to show up to the big game and have it be as cool as you want it to be.”

Brill will round out this year with another supporting turn in a big film. In Sian Heder’s crowd-pleasing biopic “Being Heumann,” he plays Gene Eidenberg, a real-life political adviser who kind of takes the heat when Mark Ruffalo’s Joseph A. Califano Jr. (the U.S. Secretary of Health, Education, and Welfare) won’t give much leeway to disability rights activist Judy Heumann and her compatriots during a historic sit-in.

“Sian’s take on the world is so cool, because she has such a good heart and is so funny and fun. The way she sees the world is so filled with light and joy, even when she’s taking on pretty heavy topics,” he said. “I don’t know that I have laughed that much on a set. I can’t remember the last time I did. Sian is so funny and fun, and so is Mark, and so is Dylan [O’Brien]. It was such a joy.”

Heder’s film is remarkable for the way it built actual access into its story about the need for more equitable access for all. Even as an able-bodied actor playing an able-bodied role, Brill felt the power of that.

“I think when the culture is about ‘let’s take care of people and meet needs,’ the work can thrive more,” he said. “I think the camaraderie amongst actors becomes very different. It becomes a lot tighter. There were these group green rooms and dressing rooms that you sort of never get. We had these lounges where we were hanging out and we were able to dissect the day, and that was really lovely. I mean, as with any movie, I think it was still really difficult at times and there are these monumental learning curves, but that’s part of the joy of filmmaking too, is that every single project is a new project. You never stop learning how to make a movie.”

And Brill knows about all kinds of projects. This is the kind of actor who pops up everywhere. A quick glance at his IMDb page is filled with delights — like the year 2017, when he appeared in not only an episode of “Law & Order: SVU,” but also “NCIS: New Orleans.” He laughed when I mentioned that double whammy.

“What was really cool was that I couldn’t have played more different characters,” he said. “I was like a coke dealer who lived in Soho in ‘SVU,’ and in ‘NCIS,’ I was a spirit medium who thought that he was a con artist, but then started actually communing with spirits. ‘NCIS: New Orleans,’ I filmed four days and was in New Orleans for three weeks, so I just had all this free time to explore New Orleans for the first time. It was incredible.”

Brill, it seems, finds value — of all kinds — in every project and part. So, is there some sort of magic balance he wants to strike with his choices? Is there a way to plot this kind of trajectory?

“It’s really tough to say, because there’s no continuity, it always changes,” Brill said. “But I have been lucky enough to really find a family in theater in New York, and so I do feel like it is there for me on some level. There are definitely things that I really want to do. There are challenges that I want to give myself, and I would say that the most open plane for that right now is television. I really want to find out what it’s like to play a character who lives and changes over a decade. I’m desperate for that experience.”

He’d like to be able to do that and still do theater. He added, “I see my friends who are on television shows and are navigating doing theater in their off time. Michael Urie is a huge inspiration in that because he’s such a theater creature, but he’s always been on TV too. So that’s a thing that I think about a lot, is the balance.”

But what he ultimately wants is something a bit harder to pin down, a balance that goes beyond designations like “film” or “TV show” or “theater,” the kind of spot that values experience in all its shapes. And, yes, probably the kind of space in which spending time with his cat is just as rewarding as a varied resume and making stuff with friends.

“I feel like life is long and I’m here for the challenge, and I’m going to get to do all of it. I’m just biding my time,” Brill said. “I feel like nowhere more than in this industry does the aphorism apply of ‘if you want to make God laugh, make plans.’ I’m down to ride the wave and let things come as they come. The most rewarded and fulfilled I’ve ever felt in this industry are the projects that are born out of tight-knit groups of friends or where tight-knit friendships are made, because what we do is storytelling, and storytelling is about creating and solidifying community. I think the thing that I will always keep wanting to do is telling stories with close friends, whatever the medium is. That’s the thing I want to do most.”

Apple will release “Being Heumann” in select theaters on Friday, November 6 and on Apple TV on Friday, November 13. A Blue Harbor Entertainment and Variance Films release, “The Musical” is currently available to rent or buy digitally on major streaming and VOD storefronts.

entry.title: ‘Cherry & Virgin’ Review: A Fantastic Indie Anime Blends Different Art Styles and a Slew of Pop Culture References into an Innovative Modern Rom-Com
entry.summary: An erotic manga artist who's never had sex falls in love with a similarly inexperienced illustrator in Masanao Kawajiri's standout anime.
entry.content:
“I draw erotic manga but have never even held a woman’s hand,” admits Ryo (Takashi Okado) at the start of “Cherry & Virgin,” a charming and cuttingly funny diagnosis of two lonely hearts and their mutual struggles with intimacy. He and the part-time fujoshi artist Ami (Yaeko Kiyose) have met on the apps, their feelings of isolation shown in the fact that they’re from different worlds — or so it appears on screen

The most immediately striking element of director Masanao Kawajiri’s crowd-funded film — made with support from Toei, who are thanked in a winking moment that just about stays on the far side of the fourth wall) — is how the characters depicted in the style of art they are most closely associated with. Ryo is in sketchy but more naturalistic black and white and textured with screen-tone, resembling something like the more “realist” manga artists he name-checks, such as Inio Asano. Ami is shown in fully stylized color, illustrated in in closer proximity to the sort of BL (“boys love”) characters which she might draw and upload to Pixiv.

Related Stories
‘Caligula’ Director Tinto Brass Dies at 93
‘The Greatest’ Review: Amazon’s Handsome Muhammed Ali Biopic Connects in Spite of Itself

On their date, the two also exists in background matching the style in which they’re drawn, and the room they share is divided by these different viewpoints. Where the film really impresses is how this unique approach never just feels like a gimmick, instead it feels like a tool by which to offer incredibly direct access to the feelings and personalities of these characters; during the aforementioned first date in the bar, the art styles in which they’re depicted begin to merge as the two come to closer understanding of the other.

In flashbacks and in other moments, the design of Ryo and Ami often shifts — their styles swap when they first kiss, and in flashbacks they are drawn in a cruder and more childlike style. In Ami’s case this goes back even further. A simplified drawing style that feels lifted from Microsoft Paint also reflects her own imposter syndrome about her art; it comes with a memory of being bullied by a more accomplished artist, like who is drawn with more technical detail in the same scene, and then her own mother berating her about it the same day. It’s a very pure kind of animated expression which never limits itself to any one formal constraint (a couple of sequences even use puppet theatre).

This approach goes far beyond just the two main characters, as the film’s supporting cast includes cartoon animals, mecha and even 3D VTuber avatar (the latter particularly jarring as they walk into an otherwise 2D setting). A lot of the animation itself in “Cherry and Virgin” embraces rotoscoping, though limiting the number of drawings to an extent that it skirts around the sense of sense of uncanniness which can sometimes emerge from the method. Because of how the film so brazenly mixes so many art styles and even mediums, the rotoscoping feels like a natural fit rather than some kind of awkward superimposition.

In the spirit of the patchwork art direction of the film, which often also incorporates the language of manga panelling itself into the frame, Kawajiri also occasionally further peels back the layer of illustration – or illusion, perhaps – to show the actors in live-action, though only in brief moments. Similarly, there are segments in “Cherry and Virgin” where a color tool is visible on screen when the background changes.

Kaga Misato’s screenplay finds the charm in such antics with both characters even as they confront the worst aspects of themselves, particularly in Ryo’s case, who spends much of the film deprogramming himself from the incel rhetoric creeping in to his reflections on dating. Part of his journey is his self-examination of no small amount of misogyny simmering under the surface, and what works about “Cherry & Virgin”is just how frank the film is about how ugly Ryo’s worst tendencies are – ones he does identify in himself and immediately work to rectify – particularly when it comes to dismissing women as characters passing through his life. Being honest about this side of him it makes the later intimacy feel less phony, more vulnerable, and ultimately more romantic. If there was any knock against the film as a whole it’s that sometimes Ami’s perspective does, ironically, take up a little less space than his. But not that Ami is an afterthought, she also has plenty of anxieties of her own which manifest in the film’s constantly shifting imagery and her awareness of her friends’ lives moving forward while she remains static.

Kawajiri crashes the two together both with a rather sweet, tentative courtship and plenty of comedy around the anxiety which would accompany any new romance, let alone one between two shut-ins with no game. One great running gag revolves around what Ryo and his friends refer to as the “Safe Sex Incident” (a double entendre) which returns in live-action insert shots, and once more with phenomenal timing in one prolonged moment of embarrassment for Ryo. Another delightful touch throughout the film’s runtime is how, just in the same way that Kawajiri represents characters through the art-style associated with them, he also creates visual understanding of them through dozens upon dozens of homages to decades of cultural ephemera associated with otaku.

No matter how esoteric the reference, it’s always in service of the tone of the scene itself or adds another layer to one of the characters. For a more familiar example, Ryo’s view of his father is represented by the latter being drawn as the famously bad dad from “Neon Genesis Evangelion,”Gendo Ikari. (Anno’s work and the heyday of Gainax in general is all over this film, both in terms of its chosen topic of angry otaku, and the deployment of mixed media in its romantic comedy). Friends comfort each other through quoting Mamoru Oshii. It’s all part of a shared language between the characters which is also open to an unfamiliar audience, to Kawajiri’s credit – even though there are so many it never becomes a secret code to alienate those who know from those who don’t (at one point the Ghanaian pallbearers appear, so it’s not all nods to old manga and anime), but it does make for some great extra laughs on top of the more traditional pratfalls and and gags.

“All drawings are lies,” Ryo says in a debate with Ami about what they prefer in how they capture a person or a character, later saying that his style keeps changing in his pursuit of something “novel.” “Cherry & Virgin” is hardly a cop-out by showing all of these different avenues in close proximity as part of its love story, one about seeing all the sides of a person and not just their idealized self. Through those “lies, as Ryo calls them, and by virtue of putting all of these radically different approaches into close proximity, the filmfeels more truthful as a result, a quality highlighted by its moving and often deeply funny script.

Grade: A

“Cherry & Virgin” premiered at the 2026 Tokyo International Film Festival. It is currently seeking U.S. distribution.

entry.title: Alan Cumming Says ‘Tip Toe’ Was His Greatest Role Ever — but He Never Wants to Think About It Again
entry.summary: Cumming tells IndieWire all about that devastating finale and why this role made his career.
entry.content:
[Editor’s note: The following interview contains spoilers for “Tip Toe,” including its finale.]

Most viewers these days know Alan Cumming for hanging out with Traitors, in one of television’s most addictive reality shows. But recently, he took on a role of a lifetime in limited series “Tip Toe,” in which he plays Leo, a queer bartender with a heart of gold whose life is cut short when he tries to strike up a friendship with his volatile and bigoted neighbor, Clive.

The five-episode limited series takes viewers on an emotional journey, opening with a shocking first scene which is also how the series ends. Leo has been hung outside his house, with Clive and a group of men looking on. Leo’s story is beautifully devastating, and the finale is one hour of gutting television.

Related Stories
‘The Greatest’ Review: Amazon’s Handsome Muhammed Ali Biopic Connects in Spite of Itself
The Mad (Color) Science Behind Rian Johnson’s New Camera App

Cumming recently sat down with IndieWire to discuss the finale and why he now needs to let Leo go.

Created and written by Russell T. Davies of “Doctor Who” fame, “Tip Toe” follows Leo and Clive (David Morrissey) in the days leading up to Leo’s brutal death at Clive’s hands. The show is not only filled with trauma, but deep joy, especially in showing the friendship between Leo and George, Clive’s teenage son, who is grappling with his own secret about his sexuality.

Davies can’t say enough good things about Cumming, and revealed that he took the entire young cast to a Lady Gaga concert as a bonding experience. Cumming confessed that he and Davies had been trying to work together for years, but it never worked out timing wise, until “Tip Toe.” Let’s just say Davies had Cumming at hello.

“Nine months before, we had a Zoom, and I simply described scene one of ‘Tip Toe,’ and from that moment on we had him,” Davies said, lighting up as he recalling the chat. He added that Cumming kept his schedule free a year before for filming the series.

“It’s the thing I’m most proud of in my career acting-wise,” Cumming said. “It was so grueling and traumatic to make.” He added that he didn’t really have to do extra research, because he lived through a lot of what Leo lived through. “I’ve never really played a part where I was able to bring so much of my own life, my own experience to the screen,” he said.

He also sees why Leo tried to trust Clive so much. “I understand everything Leo did. I let people behave badly for too long,” Cumming said. “I try to see the best in people … thinking you can fix people. And also, just being sort of a people-pleaser.”

Cumming said his favorite experience making the show was when the cast came to see his play in Scotland, and then came up for a weekend to his house in the Highlands. As for those grueling, traumatic end scenes, Cumming said, “The football boys who had to kill me were so supportive during filming.” With each terrible scene, they would stop and hug Cumming afterwards. “In the course of doing something about what a terrible place we are in our society, I was really heartened by working with the young people in this,” he said.

Filming the finale was not easy for any of them. “The hanging scene was just awful to do. It was so long, took so many days. The actual going up, and being hung, it was so traumatic. I didn’t realize how traumatized I was by it, until it came out. As soon as it finished [filming], I’ve never wanted to get away from a character as much as Leo. As much as I loved him. It was so heavy on my shoulders,” Cumming said.

But the true heart of the show, according to Cumming, is Davies’ writing. “It could easily be horrible straight guy and battered gay guy. What’s so brilliant about the writing is you can see blame and fault in both ways. But also, goodness in both,” he said.

In many ways, the show couldn’t have come at a better time. Cumming said, “It’s so prescient. We have allowed hateful rhetoric to become normalized. To the point that, we don’t bat an eye when really awful things happen. … Hopefully, this will be a conversation starter.”

For Cumming’s breakdown of the finale, watch the full interview in the video above.

All five episodes of “Tip Toe” are streaming now on Starz.

entry.title: ‘Caligula’ Director Tinto Brass Dies at 93
entry.summary: Tinto Brass, an Italian filmmaker who made erotic movies like 'Caligula,' died at age 93.
entry.content:
Giovanni “Tinto” Brass, an avant-garde filmmaker best known for directing the X-rated historical epic “Caligula,” has died. He was 93 years old. His wife Caterina Varzi and children Bonifacio and Beatrice Brass told Italian news agency Ansa that Brass had died, but did not give a cause.

Brass’ career kicked off in the 1960s and ’70s with a series of experimental films including his debut, “Who Works Is Lost,” which followed a day in the life of an unemployed designer. It screened at the 1963 Venice Film Festival. Other early works includes “Yankee,” a 1966 Western about a standoff between a bounty hunter and a crime boss, as well as “Col cuore in gola,” a 1967 murder mystery which featured Jean-Louis Trintignant.

With 1976’s “Salon Kitty,” a historical drama set in a Berlin brothel during the Nazi era, Brass moved into erotic filmmaking. But it was “Caligula,” an infamous look at one of Rome’s most notorious emperors, that made a name for Brass. The film was written by Gore Vidal, who later disavowed it, and produced by Penthouse founder Bob Guccione. It featured a cast of esteemed actors such as Peter O’Toole, Helen Mirren, John Gielgud, and Malcolm McDowell in the title role, but made headlines for its frank look at ancient Rome’s sexual depravity, depicting orgies and hardcore sex. “Caligula” was re-edited and re-cut several times only to bomb at the box office when it opened in the U.S. in 1980. However, it has built up a significant cult following over the decades and an 178-minute “Ultimate Cut,” premiered at the Cannes Film Festival in 2023 to a warmer reception from reviewers.

entry.title: ‘The Greatest’ Review: Amazon’s Handsome Muhammed Ali Biopic Connects in Spite of Itself
entry.summary: Produced in collaboration with the iconic athlete's estate, the eight-part series follows Ali from his Gold Medal win through his first championship.
entry.content:
In 1977, just a year after “Rocky” reinvigorated the sport of boxing from the big screen, Columbia Pictures released “The Greatest,” a biography of the man who reinvigorated the sport in real life: Muhammed Ali, then 35 years old and still fighting, played himself in the movie, alongside venerated actors like Ernest Borgnine (as his trainer Angelo Dundee), James Earl Jones (as Malcolm X), and Robert Duvall (as fight promoter Bill McDonald). Fortifying the footage from his actual fights, they helped recreate his life as a professional fighter, from winning the gold medal at the 1960 Olympics through reclaiming the title belt from George Foreman in 1974.

Related Stories
‘The Intertwining’ Review: Two Medical Students Uncover Buried Truths in Tense Psychological Drama
How to Make IndieWire a Preferred Source on Google

“You’ll see the life behind the legend — the man behind the myth,” the trailer states. “And you’ll understand why he’s called The Greatest.”

Now, nearly 50 years and roughly the same number of Ali-focused projects later, Amazon Prime Video is releasing another Ali-sanctioned biopic with the same title: “The Greatest” is a new drama series produced in collaboration with the Ali estate. Lonnie Ali, Muhammed’s wife at the time of his passing, is an executive producer, as are Hollywood heavy-hitters Michael B. Jordan and Shawn “Jay-Z” Carter.

Here, Ali is played by newcomer Jaalen Best, alongside notable names like Giovanni Ribisi (as Dundee), Dana Gourrier (as Ali’s mother Odessa), and Michael Ealy (as Malcolm X). The series starts in the same place as the film — the 1960 Olympics — and the first season wraps shortly after he claims the heavyweight title from Sonny Liston (Amin Joseph). Creator Ben Watkins said he has three seasons in mind, the last of which would take place in the mid-’70s, right around the time Ali took down Foreman.

This time the trailer states, “Discover the man who became a legend.”

Having not seen the film, I can’t say how the viewing experiences compare. (But Pulitzer Prize-winning playwright and Letterboxd patron saint of patrons Tracy Letts described the film as “a strange artifact. Part hagiography, part documentary, part dramatic reenactment…” — and I’m inclined to trust him.) Neither beats the charges of crafting a heroic, wholesome image of their financially involved subject, but the series, at least, still succeeds on its own terms by delivering what’s promised: revealing the man behind the legend — or, in an echo from five decades prior, a grounded understanding of why he’s called “The Greatest.” Paired with a convincing lead turn by Best, as well as moving work from Gourrier and especially Joseph, the earnest series overcomes its stock biopic structure to linger with viewers in a manner more pleasing than disbelieving.

Watkins’ exploration of Ali is rooted in his family, framing Muhammed’s astounding boxing abilities as inextricably linked to his upbringing: the confidence and passion of an older brother, the love and faith reflected from his mother, and the focus and vision of an artist, inherited from his father, Cassius Sr. (Omari Hardwick).

Hardwick’s initial spotlight is well-earned, as he shades a painter whose ambition was thwarted by circumstance with equal parts charm and acidity. “Cash” swings from unmistakable pride in his son’s accomplishments to despair over his own failings to achieve greatness, often at the drop of a hat (or the pour of a whiskey). He paints signs, not portraits or fine works of art, and he has a weakness for liquor, women, and violence.

After his father’s latest bender, a disgusted Cassius Jr. tells him they’re nothing alike. “I don’t smoke, I don’t drink, I don’t put my hands on women,” the professional fighter says. “Just give it time,” his father replies, with the conviction of a man speaking directly to his younger self. “The Greatest” never follows up on Cash’s assertion. If anything, it implies Cassius escapes these inherited demons by defending his mother, choosing the righteous path, and earning glory in the ring so he can exemplify it outside the ropes.

That works just fine for this season’s noble arc, but that same polish that’s arguably warranted now does little to suggest future seasons will be willing to wrestle with whatever truth may exist in Cash’s warning. Ali’s four marriages, paternity disputes, and alleged abuse suggest a more complicated comparison that’s yet to be seen — and, given the producers, may not be acknowledged any more than Hardwick’s sanitized invocation if “The Greatest” continues.

Compared to Cash (or anyone, really), Muhammed’s brother Rudy (Kai Parham) is more of a blank slate: a fellow boxer who’s wholly supportive of his brother’s rise to glory as well as his decision to join the Nation of Islam (which Rudy, later known as Rahaman, also adopts). But despite always being at Muhammed’s side, he feels half-realized. Sharing his brother’s spiritual journey — a challenging path not only because of the national resistance from white Americans, but also from their devout-Christian parents — provides some insight into Rudy, which is again glimpsed when he gives into the inevitable jealousy of seeing someone so close to him excel at the life he wanted.

But the follow-through leaves a strange gap. Rudy is like a walking, barely talking accessory; a piece of the Muhammed Ali legend that has to be acknowledged for his part in helping shape his brother’s identity, but whose development is so diminished it invites unintended questions. (Did a late-in-life fallout with Lonnie Ali influence his limited depiction here?)

It’s a shame because “The Greatest” is at its best when casting Muhammed against rich characters. He and Odessa build a deep relationship that illustrates each of their evolving constitutions. Muhammad’s friendship with Malcolm X is slow and steady, sparked by recognition in small moments and a thorough understanding of their larger-than-life experiences in the public eye. Best of all is his biggest adversary, Sonny Liston, whose luckless early years spoil a tender soul Joseph keenly brings to light. It’s easy to see why Ali, with the faith of his family and support from his community, triumphs in the ring over a man whipped by his father, abandoned by society, and turned into a villain by the media.

Ali and Liston’s juxtaposition is powerful, even if “The Greatest” maroons its chief antagonist too quickly after building him up so fully. There’s clearly more to his story than the show can make time for, an inevitability “The Greatest” struggles to settle with its main subject, as well. Best is commanding as Ali, growing into his camera-friendly showmanship but maintaining the inherent mettle needed to back it up. By the time his story comes full circle, from one daunting challenge (the Olympics) to the next (his first championship belt), Muhammed’s repressed fears don’t need the exposition lent via black-and-white, mid-fight hallucinations of his family and friends, urging him on to greatness.

The message is direct. The takeaway is simple. He was a man before he became a legend, and there’s much to admire about Ali’s inner spirit, his clarity of vision, and his staggering perseverance that “The Greatest” does a fine job unpacking.

In that way, it’s not far removed from the original “Rocky.” In other, less satisfying ways, it’s not far removed from “The Greatest.” Here’s hoping Season 2 is even better.

Grade: B-

“The Greatest” premieres Wednesday, November 4 on Amazon Prime Video. All eight episodes will be released at once.
